displayQuote: Figures Don't Lie, But Liars Do Figure

meta.title: Who really said "Figures Don’t Lie, But Liars Do Figure"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Carroll D. Wright, not Mark Twain. The proverb is in print unattributed by 1884, five years before Wright’s famous speech.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Figures Don’t Lie, But Liars Do Figure'?
meta.ogDescription: An anonymous American proverb from 1884. Wright quoted it in 1889 and called it “a new saying” — then got the credit anyway.

answer.label: Nobody, traceably — an anonymous American proverb
answer.sourceLine: The saying was already circulating before any of the men credited with it used it. Its earliest known printing, in a North Dakota paper in February 1884, runs it in with a handful of other aphorisms and names nobody. When the statistician Carroll D. Wright used it five years later in his opening address to a national convention of labour statisticians, he introduced the punchline as “a new saying” — which is an author disclaiming authorship. The credit attached to him anyway, within six years.
answer.confidenceText: Wright is credited because he said it well, not because he said it first

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Grand Forks Daily Herald — “The Fire Laddies: The Great Public Benefit”
29 February 1884, page 1, Grand Forks, North Dakota — no attribution
25 June 1889, opening address to the Convention of Commissioners of Bureaus of Statistics of Labor
“a new saying” — he claimed no credit for it

source.excerpt: The old saying is that “figures will not lie,” but a new saying is “liars will figure.” It is our duty, as practical statisticians, to prevent the liar from figuring; in other words, to prevent him from perverting the truth, in the interest of some theory he wishes to establish. We can only do this by being absolutely fair ourselves.
trail: The chronology, from 1852 precursors to the 1913 Mark Twain misattribution, is Quote Investigator’s ↗. Its earliest full-proverb citation is the Grand Forks Daily Herald of 29 February 1884, where the line sits among unattributed aphorisms; its conclusion is that the saying “is not attributed to anyone in the earliest occurrences” and that Wright “did use the saying during a high-profile speech in 1889, but he did not craft it.”

Wright’s own words are the strongest evidence against his authorship. Quote Investigator quotes two published versions of the 25 June 1889 address, prefers the fuller one, and cites it to a Michigan state labour-statistics report at page 311 — the full-view volume it links ↗, which we confirmed resolves. In that version Wright labels the punchline “a new saying”.

We independently confirmed that the proverb was still circulating anonymously after Wright’s speech. The Saratoga Sun of Saratoga, Wyoming, 17 August 1899, page 4, runs a political item headed “Liars Will Figure.” ending “Figures won’t lie, but liars will figure” and credits it to another newspaper, the Douglas Budget — no Wright, no Twain. We read this in the Library of Congress’s Chronicling America page scan via its own OCR text service.

The two biggest misattributions both postdate the proverb substantially: the first ascription to Wright that Quote Investigator located is 1895, and the first to Mark Twain is a Boston medical journal of 2 October 1913 — three years after Twain’s death, and with nothing corroborating it in Twain’s own writings.
source.excerptNote: This is Wright in 1889 — the passage that made the proverb famous and got him the credit. Read the second clause again: he is quoting, not coining. The wording people use today (“figures don’t lie, but liars do figure”) is the 1884 newspaper form, not Wright’s.

source.rightsNote: The proverb’s earliest documented printing is an 1884 newspaper item and Wright’s speech was published in an 1890 state government report — both far earlier than the 1931 United States cutoff, and both in the public domain. The 1899 Saratoga Sun page quoted above is likewise public domain. No author has ever been identified to hold rights in the sentence itself.

author.name: Carroll D. Wright
author.kicker: The man it is credited to
author.heading: About Carroll D. Wright
author.metaLine: 1840–1909 · American statistician & first U.S. Commissioner of Labor
author.bio: Carroll Davidson Wright was an American statistician and the first U.S. Commissioner of Labor, serving from 1885 to 1905. He enlisted as a private in 1862, left the Civil War a colonel, sat in the Massachusetts Senate, and ran the Massachusetts Bureau of Statistics of Labor before taking charge of the Eleventh Census in 1893. He chaired the commission investigating the 1894 Pullman Strike and later became president of Clark College. His professional creed was that honest statistics are a defence against dishonest argument — which is exactly why this proverb stuck to him.

copyAttribution: This is an anonymous American proverb. Quote Investigator's earliest printing is the Grand Forks Daily Herald of 29 February 1884, where it appears among other aphorisms with no author named. The statistician Carroll D. Wright used it in his opening address to the Convention of Commissioners of Bureaus of Statistics of Labor on 25 June 1889 — but called it “a new saying”, crediting himself with nothing: “The old saying is that 'figures will not lie,' but a new saying is 'liars will figure.'”

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: A proverb about the misuse of numbers has been misattributed with some consistency. Four names have carried it; the earliest printing carries none.

items.tag: Quoted it in 1889 — and said so
items.why: Wright used the proverb in his opening address to the Convention of Commissioners of Bureaus of Statistics of Labor on 25 June 1889, introducing the punchline as “a new saying”. By 1895 The Inland Printer was calling it “Carroll D. Wright’s saying”, and an 1898 New Hampshire state report declared flatly that “It was he who originated the now famous and much misquoted saying.”

items.tag: First credited in 1913 — after his death
items.why: The earliest Twain ascription Quote Investigator located is the Boston Medical and Surgical Journal of 2 October 1913, calling it “that other famous saying of Mark Twain”. Twain died in April 1910 ↗, three years earlier, and there is no corroborating evidence in his own writings. Wikiquote’s sourced Twain page ↗ does not carry it either.

Some reference works credit the Ohio congressman, nicknamed “Old Figures”. Quote Investigator found no solid evidence — and notes the telling detail that when James Tanner used the proverb at a 1910 banquet in Grosvenor’s presence, he called it an “old-time maxim, as old as the ages” rather than crediting the man sitting there.
A 1910 volume of railway-commission proceedings attributed it to “late James G. Blaine” — one more posthumous credit, twenty-six years after the proverb was already in print.

misattribution.truthLine: The oldest known printing, in the Grand Forks Daily Herald of 29 February 1884, gives no author at all — and the man usually credited called the line “a new saying” when he borrowed it five years later. Quote Investigator ↗: “QI has not found any solid evidence for crediting the phrase to any specific individual.”

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The proverb arrived with official statistics themselves. The 1870s and 1880s were when American states and then the federal government built permanent statistical bureaus — Wright ran Massachusetts’s from 1873 and became the first U.S. Commissioner of Labor in 1885 — and the question of whether their numbers could be trusted was live and partisan. The wordplay — same two words, swapped around — put the problem in seven words: the arithmetic is innocent, the arithmetician may not be.

Which is why the attribution to Carroll D. Wright was so easy to believe. He ran the first federal labour statistics office, and he used the line to tell his own profession that its duty was “to prevent the liar from figuring”. It is the perfect quotation for him — it simply was not his.
detailsBody: Quote Investigator traces the idea back through pedestrian ancestors that lack the wordplay: an 1852 congressional debate (“figures never lie, though men sometimes do”), an 1852 magazine essay wrestling with the proverb “figures won’t lie”, and an 1854 Hartford paper’s “Figures won’t lie; but men that draw up the tables may.” The compressed modern form appears fully formed in 1884 and then spreads fast — a July 1888 Los Angeles lecture, an October 1888 Sacramento free-trade argument, and a string of 1889–1890s uses with no author attached.

The form itself is unstable, which is part of why the credit wanders. As Quote Investigator notes, the first half appears as figures won’t lie, can not lie, don’t lie, do not lie, will not lie and would not lie; the second as liars do figure, will figure, can figure, sometimes figure and figure. The version in this page’s title is the 1884 newspaper’s. Wright’s was “liars will figure”, and the 1899 Wyoming item we read used his wording while crediting a different newspaper entirely.
context.pull: The man credited with it called it “a new saying” — five years after it was already in print.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator's earliest full-proverb citation is the Grand Forks Daily Herald, 29 February 1884, p. 1, unattributed; it quotes Wright's 25 June 1889 address ('The old saying is that "figures will not lie," but a new saying is "liars will figure."') from the Michigan Seventh Annual Report p. 311, dates the first Wright credit to 1895 and the first Mark Twain credit to the Boston Medical and Surgical Journal of 2 October 1913, notes Grosvenor and Blaine credits lack solid evidence, and concludes Wright 'did not craft it' and that QI 'has not found any solid evidence for crediting the phrase to any specific individual'.

This Google Books volume ID resolves to a full-view volume titled "Documents Accompanying the Journal of the House" (Michigan. Legislature) - the volume Quote Investigator links for Wright’s 1889 opening address, cited by QI at page 311. Volume identity and full-view status confirmed here; search-inside was blocked from this environment, so the page-311 wording rests on QI’s citation rather than our own read.

Carroll Davidson Wright (25 July 1840 - 20 February 1909) was an American statistician, the first U.S. Commissioner of Labor 1885-1905, chief of the Massachusetts Bureau of Statistics of Labor 1873-1878, in charge of the Eleventh Census from 1893, chairman of the 1894 Pullman Strike commission and later president of Clark College.
Samuel Langhorne Clemens ("Mark Twain") lived 30 November 1835 to 21 April 1910, which places the 2 October 1913 ascription three years after his death.

Wikiquote's Mark Twain page carries no version of 'figures don't lie, but liars do figure'; its only related sourced entry is Twain on figures beguiling him and the 'lies, damned lies, and statistics' remark he attributed to Disraeli.

The Saratoga Sun (Saratoga, Wyoming), 17 August 1899, page 4, carries an item headed 'Liars Will Figure.' ending 'Figures won't lie, but liars will figure. Douglas Budget.' - the proverb in anonymous circulation ten years after Wright's speech, credited to another newspaper rather than to any person. Read via the Library of Congress Chronicling America OCR text service for that page scan.
